Article Title: South Korean lawmaker denied US visa for 1991 conviction. Three days later, he was issued A-2 visa after Marco Rubio's diplomatic intervention
Article Text:
South Korean lawmaker was denied a diplomatic US visa apparently for his past conviction dating back to the 1990s.

What happened in the visa controversy?

What was the South Korean lawmaker convicted of?

A South Korean lawmaker who was initially denied a US visa over a decades-old criminal conviction was issued an official A-2 visa three days later, following diplomatic intervention involving US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.Jin Sung-joon, chairman of South Korea's National Assembly National Defense Committee and a member of the ruling Democratic Party, received his visa from the US Embassy in Seoul on October 31, after his initial application was refused on October 28.The controversy centred on Jin's 1991 conviction under South Korea's National Security Act, for which he was sentenced to three years in prison and a three-year suspension of his civil rights. The exact reason for the initial visa refusal was not officially confirmed, although the lawmaker's past conviction was widely cited as a possible factor.Jin was seeking an A-2 visa, a category issued to foreign government officials travelling to the United States on official government business. He was scheduled to join a bipartisan South Korean parliamentary delegation visiting the US Indo-Pacific Command in Hawaii from November 1 to 5.Jin announced the initial rejection on October 28 through a Facebook post, sharing what appeared to be a US visa refusal notice.He expressed strong regret over the decision, saying it was difficult to understand how the US could deny his application when he had previously visited the US Pacific Command in March 2014 as a member of a parliamentary committee.Jin said US authorities had requested court documents relating to his 1991 conviction, following which he submitted the relevant ruling.The case triggered diplomatic intervention from Seoul. South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul reportedly raised the matter with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth when the two met in the Philippines on October 28.South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun also raised the issue with Rubio on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta on October 30.On October 31, Rubio acknowledged the visa issue during a press conference in Atlanta, saying it appeared to involve an individual's actions from decades ago."I think there was one particular visa individually that there was an issue about regarding behavior perhaps a couple decades ago, but we'll work through that at a bilateral basis, not in a press conference," Rubio said.He indicated that the matter would be addressed through bilateral consultations between the two countries.Later that day, Jin announced that the US Embassy in Seoul had issued his A-2 visa, three days after the initial refusal."It is fortunate that the US State Department has issued the official A-2 visa, albeit belatedly," he said in his Facebook post.Jin was convicted in 1991 of violating South Korea's National Security Act. He was sentenced to three years in prison and a three-year suspension of his qualifications.According to South Korean media reports, he was accused of organizing a group during his military service that spread anti-American and pro-North Korean views, including calls for the withdrawal of US troops from South Korea.He was pardoned and had his rights restored in 1995 as part of a special presidential pardon marking South Korea's Liberation Day.Jin has questioned why the decades-old conviction should affect his official visit, particularly given his previous visit to the US Pacific Command.The lawmaker departed for Hawaii on November 1 with a bipartisan delegation that included Democratic Party lawmakers Kim Byung-joo and Jin himself, along with People Power Party lawmaker Lim Jong-deuk and Reform Party lawmaker Chun Ha-ram. The delegation is scheduled to meet senior US military officials, including the commander of the US Pacific Command, to discuss bilateral security cooperation.
Article Summary: Jin Sung-joon was convicted in 1991 of violating South Korea's National Security Act. He was sentenced to three years in prison and a three-year suspension of his civil rights. The lawmaker was seeking an A-2 visa, a category issued to foreign government officials travelling to the United States on official government business.

US President Donald Trump targeted Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday, repeatedly calling the Michigan progressive a “jihadist” and making remarks about his Muslim faith as voters prepare to head to the polls for Tuesday’s midterm elections.Trump's comments came as El-Sayed remains in a closely contested Michigan Senate race against Republican candidate Mike Rogers. Article Title: An Indiana father lost his $350,000-a-year job after 26 years and moved to Virginia for work; an October 29 court upheld giving his ex-wife sole legal custody of their son and ordering him to pay $4,0
Article Text:
Court found the child well-adjusted and saw no reason to relocate him.(AI image)

How Scotty's job loss led him to Virginia

Child's schooling influenced the decision

Why appeals court upheld custody and legal fees

An Indiana father who lost his $350,000-a-year job after 26 years and moved to Virginia for new employment has lost his appeal against a court decision giving his former wife sole legal custody and primary physical custody of their son.Scotty G Nabors challenged the custody arrangement and an order requiring him to pay $4,000 towards his ex-wife's legal fees. However, the Indiana Court of Appeals upheld both decisions on Thursday, finding that the changes were supported by evidence and were in the child's best interests.Nabors and his former wife, Jill A Nabors, divorced in December 2024, according to the details mentioned in the ruling . At the time, both lived in Bartholomew County, Indiana, and agreed to share responsibility for their son, who was born in July 2014. Their arrangement allowed the child to spend alternating weeks with each parent.That arrangement became difficult to maintain after both parents decided to relocate in 2025. Scotty moved to Virginia after finding another job, while Jill moved to Fairmount, Indiana, to live closer to her family. The distance between their new homes meant the existing weekly custody arrangement was no longer practical.The dispute eventually reached the courts, with both parents seeking changes to custody.Scotty wanted his son to move with him to Virginia, while Jill argued that the child should remain in Indiana.Scotty had worked for Cummins for 26 years before losing his job in March 2025. At the time of his termination, he earned approximately $350,000 annually, excluding bonuses.The couple disagreed over why he had lost his job. Scotty claimed Jill had sent photographs to his employer that made it appear he was drinking at work. Jill maintained that his drinking had caused his dismissal.During court proceedings, Scotty acknowledged previously consuming 1.75 litres of Jack Daniel's whiskey every one to two weeks. However, he said his drinking had decreased and denied consuming alcohol while working.After receiving a severance package, Scotty initially remained in Indiana and searched for employment. Unable to find a comparable position, he accepted a job with American Woodmark Corporation in Virginia, earning approximately $280,000 annually without bonuses.He moved to Stephens City in August 2025 and purchased a four-bedroom house with his new wife. The property included a separate bedroom for his son, and Scotty told the court that the neighbourhood offered good schools and activities for children.Meanwhile, Jill had moved to Fairmount with her new husband, whom she married in February 2025.Following her move, Jill enrolled her son at Park Elementary School without Scotty's consent. Court records showed that the child had adjusted well to the new school, made friends and received all A grades and one B-minus during his first semester.The child also enjoyed living at his mother's property and continued meeting a close friend from Columbus approximately once a month.Although Scotty believed his son's academic performance had declined, Jill disputed this. The trial court found that the child was doing well in his new surroundings and saw no reason to move him away from his school and friends.The court also examined the parents' strained relationship. Evidence showed that both had behaved poorly towards each other, sometimes in their son's presence.In one incident in May 2025, Scotty took the child out of school without informing Jill or the school. When Jill could not contact him, she requested a police welfare check. Scotty later acknowledged that failing to notify the school was his mistake.In March 2026, the trial court awarded Jill sole legal custody and primary physical custody, while allowing Scotty parenting time under a revised arrangement.Scotty challenged the decision, arguing that the court had focused too heavily on his behaviour while giving insufficient attention to Jill's actions. He also raised concerns about her new husband's previous battery conviction and requested a more structured schedule for telephone and video contact with his son.The appeals court rejected his arguments, finding that the lower court had considered the child's relationships, schooling, living arrangements and the parents' inability to communicate respectfully.It also upheld the $4,000 legal-fee award. Scotty earned approximately $5,384 weekly, compared with Jill's $825, and the judges found that this income difference supported the order.The court therefore concluded that the custody changes were justified by the parents' relocation and the child's circumstances.
Article Summary: Scotty G Nabors lost his appeal against a court decision giving his former wife sole legal custody and primary physical custody of their son. He challenged the custody arrangement and an order requiring him to pay $4,000 towards his ex- wife's legal fees. However, the Indiana Court of Appeals upheld both decisions on Thursday, finding that the changes were supported by evidence.

Article Title: A Kentucky landowner paid $800,000 in 1998 for two acres beside the Ohio River despite floodplain rules adopted a year earlier; after never seeking a floodplain variance, it lost its compensation appe
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

A development plan approved before floodplain restrictions

Landowner purchased the property after restrictions

Court says compensation claim was premature

Ruling leaves possibility of a future lawsuit

Buying land for development can involve risks that are not immediately visible, particularly when local regulations restrict how a property can be used. A Kentucky landowner that purchased a two-acre tract along the Ohio River for $800,000 in 1998 has lost its appeal seeking compensation over floodplain restrictions that it claimed prevented the planned development. The dispute centred on floodplain regulations introduced by local authorities in 1997, which limited construction in certain areas considered vulnerable to flooding.In an opinion rendered on October 30, 2026, the Kentucky Court of Appeals affirmed a Jefferson Circuit Court decision granting summary judgment to Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government and the Metropolitan Sewer District. According to the court's ruling , available on Justia under Lampton Securities Partnership, LLP v. Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government, the landowner had not obtained a final decision from the relevant authorities about what could be built on the property. It had also failed to seek a variance, an administrative exception that could have allowed development despite the restrictions. The appellate court consequently concluded that the compensation claim was premature.The dispute originated in the early 1990s, when the owners of a roughly four-acre property along the Ohio River received approval from the Metropolitan Sewer District for a condominium development.The project was planned in two phases, with the first covering approximately two acres and the second intended for the remaining two acres. While the first phase was completed, the second portion, which later became the subject of the legal dispute, remained undeveloped. An electrical equipment building was constructed on the tract, and utility lines were installed, but no condominiums were built there.In 1997, Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government introduced floodplain ordinances following catastrophic flooding. The regulations restricted most new construction within the conveyance zone, a designated section of the floodplain intended to accommodate the movement of floodwater. The two-acre tract was located within this zone.The ordinances, however, included exceptions. They allowed certain construction that had already begun before the regulations took effect to continue. They also permitted affected property owners to apply for specific variances through the Metropolitan Sewer District's Floodplain Board.Lampton Securities Partnership purchased the two-acre tract in 1998 for $800,000, a year after the floodplain regulations were introduced. The tract sat largely idle for years before the partnership placed it on the market around 2019. The marketing materials described the land as suitable for commercial development. However, Metropolitan Sewer District personnel learned about the sale, leading to a meeting between the district's legal counsel and representatives of Lampton.During the meeting, the district's counsel expressed the view that the floodplain ordinances prevented development on the property. Lampton subsequently argued that the restrictions had deprived it of all economically beneficial uses of the land. Rather than applying for a variance or attempting to begin the second phase of the previously approved condominium project, the partnership filed a reverse condemnation lawsuit against the Metro Government and the Metropolitan Sewer District in May 2020.Reverse condemnation, also known as inverse condemnation, allows a property owner to seek compensation when government regulations or actions effectively take private property without formally acquiring it. Lampton argued that the restrictions amounted to such a taking.In July 2025, the Jefferson Circuit Court granted summary judgment in favour of the two government entities. The lower court cited Lampton's failure to exhaust administrative remedies and the timing of its complaint. The partnership appealed, but the Kentucky Court of Appeals found that the case could be dismissed on another ground: the claim was not ripe for judicial review.The appellate judges explained that a regulatory taking cannot be established until the relevant authorities have made a final decision about how a property can be used. Property owners must generally follow reasonable administrative procedures, including pursuing available variance procedures, before claiming that regulations have eliminated the property's economic value.In this case, Lampton had received no final decision from the Floodplain Board. The court also noted that an opinion expressed by a Metropolitan Sewer District staff member was not an official determination of the property's permitted uses. The court rejected Lampton's argument that seeking a variance would have been futile. The Floodplain Board had the authority to grant exceptions, and the record showed that it had approved variances for other property owners.The Court of Appeals also found insufficient evidence to establish that the Floodplain Board would inevitably reject Lampton's application. The district's representative had testified that the decision rested with the board, not individual staff members, and that no similar condominium development variance had previously been requested. The judges therefore concluded that Lampton had filed its compensation lawsuit before obtaining a final administrative decision on the property's permitted uses. They affirmed the Jefferson Circuit Court's summary judgment in favour of Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government and the Metropolitan Sewer District.Importantly, the ruling did not determine whether the property could ultimately be developed or whether the floodplain regulations amounted to a taking. The appellate court clarified that Lampton could bring another compensation claim in the future if it obtained a final administrative decision and its claim otherwise met the legal requirements.
Article Summary: Kentucky landowner lost its appeal seeking compensation over floodplain restrictions that it claimed prevented the planned development. The dispute centred on floodplain regulations introduced by local authorities in 1997, which limited construction in certain areas considered vulnerable to flooding. Kentucky Court of Appeals affirmed a Jefferson Circuit Court decision granting summary judgment to Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government and the Metropolitan Sewer District.

Article Title: Watch: Homes submerged, residents rescued as torrential rains trigger floods in US, Mexico
Article Text:
Cars submerged, swept into sea as flash floods

Mexico: Flash floods sweep cars away in Los Cabos

Heavy rains have triggered flash floods and river flooding across parts of the US Southwest and Mexico, forcing evacuations and rescue operations. While emergency teams have been rescuing residents in flood-hit communities in the US, videos from Mexico showed powerful floodwaters sweeping away cars.Hurricane Simon battered Mexico’s Pacific coast on October 12 with heavy rain and strong winds, while Tropical Storm Rachel brought heavy rain and gusty winds to the US Southwest.Arizona has reported flooding in several communities, with emergency teams rescuing people trapped in homes and carrying out boat rescues, the Associated Press reported.In Pagosa Springs, a tourist town in southwestern Colorado known for its hot springs and ski resorts, officials warned of potentially catastrophic flooding as the San Juan River was forecast to reach 21.9 feet. This would exceed the 17.8 feet recorded during the devastating 1911 flood that destroyed much of the town.Flood watches and warnings were issued on Saturday for nearly all of Arizona and parts of southern Utah, southwestern Colorado, western New Mexico and southern Nevada, including the Four Corners region. The National Weather Service warned that continued rainfall could cause further flooding and make roads in remote areas impassable.A meteorologist in Tucson said the region was receiving two to three months' worth of rain within a few days. Forecasters estimated that some areas could receive up to four inches of rain, with the wet weather expected to continue through Monday.Videos from San José del Cabo in Mexico's Baja California Sur state showed powerful floodwaters sweeping cars through the Costa Azul stream as heavy rainfall turned normally dry channels into raging rivers. Torrential rain, reportedly exceeding 100 mm, also flooded roads and overwhelmed local drainage systems.A video from Los Cabos, Mexico, showed cars being swept out to sea as flash floods turned dry riverbeds into raging torrents.
Article Summary: Heavy rains have triggered flash floods and river flooding across parts of the US Southwest and Mexico. Arizona has reported flooding in several communities, with emergency teams rescuing people trapped in homes and carrying out boat rescues. In Pagosa Springs, Colorado, officials warned of potentially catastrophic flooding as the San Juan River was forecast to reach 21.9 feet.

Article Title: Netanyahu pushing Donald Trump for nuclear strike on Iran? US commentator makes big claim
Article Text:
File photo: US President Donald Trump and Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu

Carlson claims Netanyahu wants war to continue

Warning over regional and global consequences

Trump weighing diplomacy as Iran talks continue

US media personality and political commentator Tucker Carlson has claimed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing US President Donald Trump to launch a nuclear strike on Iran, alleging that Washington could take a decision on the use of nuclear weapons within days.In a detailed post on X on Monday, Carlson claimed that the proposed target could be Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence allegedly believes Tehran has restarted its nuclear enrichment programme.He argued that conventional US weapons would not be able to penetrate the mountain's granite to reach underground tunnels where enrichment activity is supposedly taking place."Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran," Carlson wrote.He further claimed that Netanyahu had been pushing for such an operation and quoted an unnamed source as saying, "Bibi calls Trump about it every day."Carlson's post did not provide independently verifiable evidence for the claims about a possible nuclear strike or the alleged pressure being exerted by Netanyahu.Carlson linked the alleged push for military action to Netanyahu's political position following last week's elections in Israel.He claimed the Israeli prime minister would struggle to form a government without Trump's direct intervention and could face investigations and possible jail if he lost office."Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war," Carlson wrote.He also alleged that several senior US officials were backing Netanyahu's position and opposed a negotiated settlement with Iran.Carlson named US defence secretary Pete Hegseth and Centcom commander Brad Cooper, while also claiming that secretary of state Marco Rubio and CIA director John Ratcliffe were following the Israeli prime minister's lead.Carlson further claimed that former US president Barack Obama had opposed the Iran peace deal being drafted in Doha during a recent meeting. He did not provide details or evidence to substantiate that assertion either.The commentator also said that Netanyahu had travelled secretly to Abu Dhabi on September 27 to seek the United Arab Emirates' support for a final military operation against Iran, but that the Emiratis had refused.Carlson warned that another escalation could have serious consequences for the Gulf region and the global economy, pointing to damage to oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and disruptions to energy and fertiliser markets.He claimed that 11 of the approximately 850 supertankers used to transport oil globally had been badly damaged in the Strait of Hormuz in October.On the consequences of a possible nuclear strike, Carlson alleged that a ground explosion at Pickaxe Mountain could contaminate the Persian Gulf and affect the water supply of 100 million people. He also warned that the use of a nuclear weapon by the US could set a precedent for other countries.Carlson claimed that Russia had told at least two governments that a US nuclear strike on Iran would give it the freedom to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. He also cited possible nuclear escalation involving North Korea and South Korea.He further alleged that the US administration had quietly revised its nuclear doctrine since February to make the first use of so-called "battlefield nukes" easier.Carlson's claims come amid ongoing diplomatic efforts to resume negotiations between Washington and Tehran, even as the possibility of renewed military action remains under discussion.US President Donald Trump and Netanyahu spoke by phone on Saturday about the state of negotiations with Iran and the possibility of returning to military operations, according to an Axios report.The report said Netanyahu was pressing Trump to launch fresh strikes after Tuesday's US midterm elections, while the US president wanted to allow negotiations to continue. An Israeli source described the conversation as "tough", while a US source called it "direct".Trump later described the conversation as a "very good talk" and confirmed that Iran was among the subjects discussed, without providing further details.Trump has said negotiations with Iran were "going fine" and that he was not "in much of a hurry". However, he also indicated that the US still needed to address one or two Iranian nuclear sites, specifically referring to Pickaxe Mountain."We can do that in 10 minutes. We have that planned. You can look at Pickaxe Mountain. We need to take care of that. We can do that very quickly," Trump said.Meanwhile, US Vice President JD Vance sent a letter last week to Iran's national security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, regarding the possibility of restarting negotiations.Qatari mediators also held discussions with Iranian officials for a third consecutive day on Sunday in an effort to facilitate an agreement to resume direct talks between Washington and Tehran.Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said no agreement had been reached and that progress depended on the US responding to Tehran's questions."We are making every effort in this regard and hope that the other side will demonstrate enough rationality to choose diplomacy over other paths," Araghchi said.Carlson, meanwhile, claimed that Trump was listening to Vance and US envoy Steve Witkoff, who he said believed a deal with Iran could still be reached.He urged the US administration to pursue diplomacy, warning against a nuclear escalation.
Article Summary: US media personality Tucker Carlson claims Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing US President Donald Trump to launch a nuclear strike on Iran. Carlson claims that the proposed target could be Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran. He claims that conventional US weapons would not be able to penetrate the mountain's granite to reach underground tunnels where enrichment activity is supposedly taking place.

Article Title: 'My body hurts, my soul hurts': Christa Pike's first statement after failed execution in US
Article Text:
Christa Pike breaks silence after botched execution

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has said she remains in constant physical and psychological pain after surviving a botched lethal injection on September 30. In her first public statement since the failed execution, the 50-year-old described her injuries, isolation in a prison hospital and uncertainty about her future.In a statement dictated to her lawyers and released on Friday, the 50-year-old said she had been struggling with pain and speech difficulties since the execution attempt.“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak,” Pike said.“And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”Pike, who is being held at the Debra K Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Tennessee, said she had prepared herself to die peacefully but instead regained consciousness alone in a hospital bed.“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next,” she said, adding that she was “searching for meaning in what happened to me”.She also expressed concern for the family of her victim, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.“I continue to think about my victim’s family,” Pike said, referring to the “terrible pain and loss they have endured”.Pike thanked the first responders and medical staff who treated her, saying support from people around the world had given her strength.“To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is something I cannot fully put into words,” she said.Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital during her scheduled execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution on September 30. Her lawyers said the injections may not have entered her bloodstream correctly, instead pooling in her arms and causing severe injuries, including burns and blistering.According to court documents, the execution team struggled to establish functioning intravenous lines. Pike reportedly complained of burning pain before losing consciousness and being transferred to a Nashville hospital in critical condition. She was discharged on October 10.Her lawyers have also asked a federal judge to end her isolation in the prison infirmary, arguing that it violates a 2024 agreement allowing her social contact with other women prisoners. They said the isolation had caused significant psychological harm.Meanwhile, a Tennessee judge has ordered officials to preserve evidence relating to the failed execution. Her lawyers have alleged that the incident violated the constitutional prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment.Governor Bill Lee has appointed a former US attorney to review the incident and suspended the state's remaining executions for the year. The move follows another problematic execution attempt in May.Lee rejected Pike's clemency appeal before the execution attempt. Asked about her sentence this week, he said, “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”Pike remains on death row. Her lawyers are seeking to have her sentence commuted to life imprisonment.
Article Summary: Christa Pike says she remains in constant physical and psychological pain after surviving a botched lethal injection on September 30. In her first public statement since the failed execution, the 50-year-old described her injuries, isolation in a prison hospital and uncertainty about her future. Her lawyers are seeking to have her sentence commuted to life imprisonment.

Article Title: A Texas man was arrested after stealing human remains from a cemetery mausoleum and throwing a bucket of bones over an FBI office fence; his mother alerted police after he asked her for money.
Article Text:
Michael Chadwick Fry. Image Credit: FOX4 News

Texas man arrested after human remains allegedly stolen from cemetery mausoleum

What led investigators to Michael Chadwick Fry

A YouTube video showed the bucket being thrown over the FBI fence

Investigators found evidence of another cemetery theft

What charges does Fry face following his arrest

Fry was previously arrested after crashing into a Dallas television station

A Texas man has been arrested after allegedly removing human remains from a cemetery mausoleum and throwing a bucket containing human bones over the fence of an FBI office in Dallas. The investigation into the incident began after the man's mother contacted police about his unusual request for money to hire a moving truck. Authorities later uncovered videos allegedly showing him with human remains at his home and carrying out the incident outside the federal building. The case has also brought renewed attention to his previous arrest in Dallas.Michael Chadwick Fry, 41, of Bartonville, Texas, was arrested on March 18, 2026, following an investigation involving the Bartonville Police Department, Denton Police Department and FBI agents.According to the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, investigators received information suggesting that Fry had unlawfully removed human remains from a cemetery in Denton County. The investigation eventually led officers to the Independent Order of Odd Fellows (IOOF) Cemetery in Denton, where they discovered a damaged mausoleum with remains missing from inside.The Denton Police Department confirmed the discovery. The department said it had been informed on March 18 that human remains recovered during an investigation by Bartonville police might have been taken from the cemetery.Following a search of the site, officers found damage to the mausoleum and confirmed that remains were missing. Authorities also said the next of kin had been notified.The case was being investigated by Bartonville police, with Denton officers providing assistance. The involvement of the FBI added a federal dimension to an investigation that began with reports of missing remains.The circumstances that brought Fry to the attention of authorities emerged through information provided by his family.According to the arrest warrant affidavit reported the Fort Worth Star-Telegram, Fry's mother contacted police on March 16 after he approached her asking for money to rent a U-Haul truck.When she asked why he needed the vehicle, he reportedly told her that he had a body that needed to be moved. His mother said he became angry and left her home after the conversation.Concerned by the statement, she contacted the Bartonville Police Department. Investigators subsequently circulated information to neighbouring law enforcement agencies to help locate Fry and watch for potentially suspicious activity.His sister also contacted authorities and provided information about a video she believed Fry had recorded and uploaded online.The footage reportedly showed him outside the FBI's Dallas field office with a bucket containing what he described as human remains. This information became an important part of the investigation and helped officers connect the cemetery case with the incident at the federal building.According to CBS News Texas, investigators reviewed a video posted on Fry's YouTube account that allegedly showed him throwing a closed white bucket over the security fence at the FBI's Dallas field office.In the footage, Fry reportedly referred to the contents as Elizabeth's remains and indicated that he wanted to attract the attention of federal agents.The arrest affidavit stated that Fry appeared to be attempting to get the FBI involved in what he considered wrongdoing by Denton County officials connected to an earlier arrest.An FBI special agent later informed investigators that the bucket contained numerous bones that appeared to be human. The remains were sent for forensic examination.Authorities also reviewed two other videos from Fry's YouTube account. These allegedly showed him holding a human skull at his residence in Bartonville. The skull reportedly had dirt, hair and other natural material still attached to it. Fry identified it as Elizabeth Virginia Lyon in the videos.According to the affidavit, an investigating officer believed the skull and the bones recovered from the FBI premises belonged to the same set of remains. However, forensic examination was needed to establish their connection.The investigation also uncovered information about a separate incident involving human remains in Oklahoma City.According to the Bartonville Police Department's statement, investigators determined that Fry had allegedly stolen an urn containing human remains from a cemetery in Oklahoma City. Police there had already opened an investigation into the theft in February 2026.Fry's mother also provided investigators with information about searches for cemeteries recorded in the vehicle he used. The GPS records reportedly showed searches for three locations, including one cemetery in Arlington, Texas, and two in Oklahoma City.She also told authorities that she had noticed a new shovel at the property and that Fry had recently started locking a backyard shed, something she said he had not regularly done before.Separately, FBI agents found evidence at the Denton cemetery suggesting that a coffin had been removed from the mausoleum.Following the investigation, Bartonville police arrested Fry at his residence in the 500 block of Oakwood Drive on March 18. According to CBS News Texas, Fry was charged with two counts of abuse of a corpse and one count of tampering with evidence, a third-degree felony under Texas law.FOX 4 reported that abuse of a corpse is a state jail felony. The charges relate to the alleged handling and removal of human remains. Court records also showed that Fry had been arrested more than two dozen times since 2003. His previous charges included assault causing bodily injury, burglary, theft, disorderly conduct, criminal mischief and resisting arrest.According to FOX 4, Fry was arrested in 2018 after repeatedly driving a rented pickup truck into the station's building while the morning news programme was being broadcast.After getting out of the vehicle, he reportedly threw sheets of paper across the pavement. He also left behind a bright orange duffel bag, prompting police to establish a security perimeter and call in a bomb squad.Investigators later determined that Fry was upset about a 2012 incident in Denton County in which sheriff's deputies fatally shot his friend during a confrontation involving a vehicle.FOX 4 reported that Fry had been a passenger in the vehicle involved in that earlier incident. Police said he was trying to attract media attention during the 2018 episode. No injuries were reported, and he was charged with criminal mischief.
Article Summary: Michael Chadwick Fry, 41, of Bartonville, Texas, was arrested on March 18, 2026, following an investigation involving the Bartonville Police Department, Denton Police Department and FBI agents. Investigators received information suggesting that Fry had unlawfully removed human remains from a cemetery in Denton County. Officers found a damaged mausoleum with remains missing from inside. The investigation also uncovered information about a separate incident involving human remains in Oklahoma City.

Article Title: Meet Connor Arbach, the 13-year-old from North Dakota who turned a bag of seasoned pretzels into a homemade snack business, selling his own flavours for $2 a bag
Article Text:
PC: Facebook/Twistology Pretzels

How 13-year-old Connor Arbach turned homemade pretzels into a small business

From ranch and dill pickle to sweet twisted churro pretzels

How Connor Arbach sells his $2 pretzel bags at local markets

A family-supported business run by a young entrepreneur

A bag of pretzels became the starting point for a small business in Fargo, North Dakota, where Connor Arbach began making his own versions of the familiar snack. According to the North Dakota Department of Agriculture, at 12, he was developing flavours, preparing batches and finding customers willing to pay $2 for a bag of his seasoned creations. What started as an interest in making pretzels has since taken shape as Twistology Pretzels, a youth-owned business with a growing selection of flavours. Connor remains involved in the work behind each packet, from experimenting with ingredients to getting the finished snacks ready for sale. His family helps with the business, which has begun appearing at local markets and community events around the Fargo-Moorhead area.Twistology Pretzels is based in Fargo, North Dakota, and is built around a relatively simple product: crunchy pretzels coated in homemade seasonings. Connor has developed a range of homemade seasonings, combining familiar savoury flavours with sweeter and spicier options.The business is run by Connor, who was 12 when he began developing the idea, with his family providing support behind the scenes. His involvement extends beyond choosing which flavours to sell.He takes part in preparing the recipes, seasoning the pretzels, baking them and packing the finished products.The range at Twistology includes familiar savoury combinations alongside flavours that take pretzels in a different direction. Ranch and Dill Pickle are among the more recognisable options, while Zesty Pizza, Honey Mustard, Chili Lime and Chipotle Barbecue offer other combinations of seasoning.There is also Twisted Churro, a sweeter option that draws on the flavour of the popular cinnamon-sugar-coated pastry. The selection gives customers a choice between tangy, spicy, savoury and sweet varieties without moving away from the basic pretzel.Homemade seasoning is central to the product. Each batch is prepared with the intention of giving the pretzels a distinct coating, rather than simply offering the familiar salted version found in most shops.According to WDAY Radio, Connor initially sold his homemade pretzels for $2 a bag, leaving them in the breakroom at his mother's workplace giving customers a straightforward way to try the different varieties. The company has been taking its products to local markets, pop-up stalls and community events across the Fargo-Moorhead area.People attending markets can see the products, choose from the available flavours and purchase them directly. For Connor, selling the snacks is also part of running the business. Making a product is only one stage of the process; getting it packaged and in front of potential buyers is another. The local events give Twistology an opportunity to build familiarity with its name and introduce its different flavours to people in the area.Although Connor is the person behind Twistology, he does not operate entirely on his own. His family helps with the business behind the scenes, supporting the work involved in preparing and selling the pretzels.Connor, however, remains closely involved in the product itself. Recipe development, seasoning, baking and packaging are all among the tasks he handles. Twistology remains a small business rooted in its local community. Its presence at Fargo-area markets and events has given it a way to introduce its products to customers while continuing to develop its range.For Connor, that idea has become a business bearing its own name, with several flavours and a $2 price tag attached to each bag.
Article Summary: Twistology Pretzels is a youth-owned business based in Fargo, North Dakota. Connor Arbach, 13, started making his own pretzels at his mother's workplace. He has developed a range of savoury and sweet flavours for the snacks. The company has been taking its products to local markets and events.

Article Title: A woman who came to Kentucky on a fiance visa signed a prenup 11 days after arriving; her husband disclosed assets above $1 million versus her $39,000, and an appeals court upheld the agreement after
Article Text:
Woman claimed pressure and limited English affected her understanding of the agreement (Representational photo)

Why Zhang challenged the agreement

Why court rejected her arguments

What judges said about her financial situation

A woman who moved from China to Kentucky on a fiance visa and signed a prenuptial agreement just 11 days after arriving in the United States has lost her attempt to overturn the agreement following her divorce.Yuancong Zhang challenged the agreement with her former husband, Stuart M Chen, whose disclosed assets exceeded $1 million, compared with her approximately $39,000. Zhang argued that she had signed the document under pressure and did not fully understand its terms because of her limited English.However, the Kentucky Court of Appeals upheld the agreement on Friday, finding no reason to overturn the family court's earlier decision.According to the judgment , the couple met in 2008, when Zhang lived in China. After several years together, they decided to marry. Before the wedding, Chen hired a lawyer in Kentucky to prepare an agreement that would protect his property for his two children. One of his children was permanently disabled and required lifelong care.The agreement stated that both Zhang and Chen would keep the property they owned before marriage, along with any property later acquired in their individual names.It also prevented either spouse from claiming a share in the increase in value of the other's property, financial support after divorce or certain benefits following the other's death.Chen gave Zhang the document in January 2015, months before she travelled to the United States. According to court records, he advised her on at least three occasions to have it translated into Chinese and explained it to her. Zhang arrived in Kentucky in July 2015, signed the agreement 11 days later and married Chen that September.The marriage continued until 2023, when Chen filed for divorce and asked the court to enforce the prenuptial agreement. Zhang opposed it, arguing that the circumstances in which she signed the document were unfair and that enforcing it would leave her struggling financially.At a hearing in April 2024, Zhang said the agreement had been presented to her in English, a language in which she was not proficient. She argued that Chen had failed to provide a Chinese translation or arrange legal representation for her.She also pointed to her immigration situation. Zhang had entered the country on a K-1 fiance visa, which required her to marry Chen within 90 days or return to China. She claimed that because the marriage depended on signing the agreement, she had little meaningful choice.Her financial position had also changed after moving to the United States. Before marriage, Zhang had worked as a journalist in China for 16 years. She was 46 at the time and, according to her testimony, had been four years away from qualifying for retirement there.Zhang did not work during the marriage until Chen filed for divorce. She told the court that her long absence from employment and limited English made finding work difficult. She eventually secured a part-time supermarket job paying approximately $100 a week and said she was applying for public assistance.The Madison Family Court ruled in October 2024 that the agreement was valid and enforceable. It subsequently applied the agreement when granting the divorce in December that year.Zhang appealed, but the appeals court agreed with the earlier decision. It noted that she had received the document approximately six months before signing it and had been repeatedly advised to seek a translation or explanation.The judges said the family court had found that Zhang had sufficient time, resources and ability to obtain help understanding the agreement but had chosen not to do so.The court also rejected her argument that making the marriage conditional on signing the agreement amounted to unlawful pressure. It explained that prenuptial agreements are permitted under Kentucky law and that insisting on such an agreement before marriage did not, by itself, establish duress.Another issue was whether Zhang should receive financial support after divorce. She argued that her age, limited English and employment difficulties meant she could not adequately support herself.However, the court found that the financial difference between the couple had existed when they married and had not materially changed during their relationship.The family court had found that Chen was retired, supported his disabled adult son and lived on his retirement assets. Zhang had a journalism degree, had recently begun working and still appeared to have some savings in China.Although Zhang claimed she had been homeless for a period after separation, the court noted that Chen had allowed her to return to his home and supported her until she found employment and an apartment.The appeals court also pointed out that Chen had signed a financial sponsorship declaration during Zhang's visa process. That obligation was separate from the prenuptial agreement, and Zhang appeared to retain the option of pursuing it through another legal action.The judges acknowledged that they might have reached a different conclusion themselves, but said the family court's findings were supported by sufficient evidence. The October 30 ruling therefore left both the prenuptial agreement and the divorce decree in place.
Article Summary: Yuancong Zhang challenged the agreement with her former husband, Stuart M Chen, whose disclosed assets exceeded $1 million, compared with her approximately $39,000. Zhang argued that she had signed the document under pressure and did not fully understand its terms because of her limited English. The Kentucky Court of Appeals upheld the agreement on Friday.

Article Title: Meet Emily Herra, 17-year-old New York student who helped turn a neglected 3,600-square-foot lot into a community garden with pollinator habitat and a 130-foot mural, then won a $10,000 prize in 2026
Article Text:
From school composting to a neighbourhood garden

When the garden disappeared overnight

More than planting trees

Recognition for a project built by young people

When Emily Herra was 12, she tried to introduce a composting programme at her school. The idea was met with resistance from administrators who believed it would be too complicated to implement. But the young New Yorker persisted, eventually getting the programme running and setting her sights on a bigger challenge: transforming a neglected patch of land in her neighbourhood into a space where people and nature are now thriving together.Five years later, the now 17-year-old has been recognised for her environmental work with the 2026 Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes. She co-founded Veggie Nuggets, a youth-led climate activism group based in Jackson Heights and the wider Queens area of New York City. Its signature project is the restoration of a previously abandoned 3,600-square-foot lot, which now features 1,800 square feet of pollinator habitat and a 130-foot climate justice mural.The prize, announced on September 15, 2026, recognises young people who have made a significant positive difference to their communities or the environment. Herra is among 15 top winners, each receiving $10,000 to support their service work or higher education, according to the award's official announcement.Herra's environmental work began with a relatively simple idea: making better use of waste. After getting the composting programme at her school off the ground, she wanted to extend her efforts beyond the campus.The opportunity came when she and her friends encountered an abandoned strip of land in Jackson Heights. The site, along 69th Street beside the CSX railway tracks, was covered in overgrown vegetation and rubbish. It was here the students saw an opportunity to create something useful for their community.A group of seven middle school students returned to clean up the area, working alongside two coaches. With guidance from master gardeners and the Jackson Heights Beautification Group, they learnt how to improve the soil and introduce native plants.The transformation required more than gardening skills. The young volunteers also had to navigate permits, applications and funding processes to secure the resources needed to maintain the space. Their work gradually turned the neglected patch into a community garden where residents could volunteer, learn about the environment and help support local biodiversity.The garden now contains a substantial pollinator habitat and a mural measuring 130 feet. The project combines environmental restoration with public art, using the space to draw attention to climate justice while creating a welcoming neighbourhood gathering point.The project did not develop without setbacks. In autumn 2024, a contractor hired by CSX cleared the strip of land, apparently unaware that the students had established a garden there. Much of their work was wiped out. In a report by The Indypendent, Herra described the destruction as one of the most difficult moments the group had experienced together. The loss threatened not only the plants and garden beds they had built, but also the time and effort the young volunteers had invested in the site.The group, however, decided to rebuild rather than abandon the project. Veggie Nuggets subsequently secured a lease with CSX, giving it recognised permission to work on the land and reducing the risk of the garden being accidentally cleared again. The group also received a grant of approximately $10,000 to purchase tools, rebuild beds, install signs and replace plants.Herra shared that the rebuilding process was still underway while she and her teammates were watching the garden return gradually, even though the work was not yet complete.The entire experience became more than just an initiative. It was the subject of 'Perennial', a documentary made by members of Veggie Nuggets. The film premiered at the Queens World Film Festival on November 8, 2025, documenting the group's response to the destruction and its efforts to restore the space.Veggie Nuggets' work extends beyond one single garden. The group organises park clean-ups, environmental workshops and community activities while advocating for sustainable practices such as composting and renewable energy. Its members have also participated in campaigns against fossil-fuel infrastructure.The organisation describes itself as a youth climate activism group working to improve neighbourhoods in Jackson Heights and Astoria. Its approach combines practical projects with advocacy, giving young people opportunities to engage with environmental issues in their own communities.Herra's work has also involved partnerships with organisations including the Jackson Heights Beautification Group and JH Scraps, a local composting initiative. Such collaborations have helped the students gain practical knowledge and access resources that would be difficult to secure on their own.“Through this experience, I’ve learned that environmental work is not just about big solutions or perfect plans,” she said. “It’s about persistence, especially when things feel slow or uncertain.”The $10,000 Gloria Barron Prize award gives Herra financial support for her continued service work or higher education. Established in 2001 by author T. A. Barron, the annual award recognises young leaders between the ages of eight and 18 across the United States and Canada.For Herra and Veggie Nuggets, the recognition highlights the role young people can play in improving their immediate surroundings. Their garden offers a practical example of how environmental work can begin with a small, overlooked space and grow into a wider community effort.
Article Summary: Emily Herra, 17, has been awarded the 2026 Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes. She co-founded Veggie Nuggets, a youth-led climate activism group based in Jackson Heights and the wider Queens area of New York City. Its signature project is the restoration of a previously abandoned 3,600-square-foot lot, which now features 1,800 square feet of pollinator habitat and a climate justice mural.

Article Title: Lady Gaga and her mother built a youth mental-health foundation; by May 2026, more than 100,000 people worldwide had earned certificates through its programme teaching how to support someone in distre
Article Text:
How Lady Gaga and her mother started the foundation

What is the Be There Certificate ?

From awareness to practical action

Why everyday support matters

Pop star Lady Gaga and her mother, Cynthia Germanotta, have spent more than a decade working to make mental-health support more accessible to young people. Their efforts reached a new milestone in May 2026, when the Born This Way Foundation announced that more than 100,000 Be There Certificates had been earned worldwide through a free online programme teaching people how to support someone struggling with their mental health.The foundation, co-founded by Gaga and Germanotta in 2012, marked the achievement in partnership with Canadian youth mental-health organisation Jack.org. The certificate programme teaches participants how to recognise signs of distress, respond with care and help someone connect with appropriate support. The foundation announced the milestone on May 31, 2026, and linked it to its Generation Be There campaign, which aims to equip young people with practical skills to support themselves and others.According to the foundation’s official impact timeline, the campaign had 186 partner organisations and attracted more than 590 attendees across its events. The initiative focuses on turning conversations about mental health into practical action, encouraging people to become more confident in supporting friends, family members and peers who may be struggling.The Born This Way Foundation was announced in January 2012 and officially launched on February 29 that year at Harvard University.The initiative grew out of Gaga’s interest in building a kinder, more accepting environment for young people, particularly those facing bullying, social pressure and difficulties with self-confidence.In the announcement published by Harvard Graduate School of Education, Germanotta said the foundation grew from her daughter’s desire to create a world in which people were accepted for who they were, regardless of their differences. She also spoke about the lasting effects young people can experience when they do not receive adequate support. The foundation initially focused on issues including wellbeing, anti-bullying, mentoring, self-confidence and youth empowerment. It brought together researchers, charitable organisations and young people to explore ways to encourage acceptance and create safer environments.Over time, mental-health awareness and support became central to its work. Rather than relying only on public awareness campaigns, the organisation developed initiatives intended to give young people tools they could use in everyday situations.The Be There Certificate is a free, self-paced online mental-health course created by Jack.org in partnership with Born This Way Foundation. It is available in English, French and Spanish and is designed to help people support someone who may be experiencing mental-health difficulties. The course centres on five principles, known as the Be There Golden Rules: “Say What You See”, “Show You Care”, “Hear Them Out”, “Know Your Role” and “Connect to Help”.The first encourages people to describe changes they have noticed without making assumptions about what someone is experiencing. The second focuses on expressing concern and showing that the person matters. Listening without judgement is another central element, alongside understanding the limits of one's role and helping someone access further support when necessary.The programme also stresses that supporting someone does not mean taking responsibility for solving all their problems. Instead, it aims to help participants recognise when a person may be struggling, respond appropriately and connect them with relevant resources. The course is educational rather than a professional qualification in mental-health care. Completing it does not make someone a therapist or replace professional assessment and treatment. Its purpose is to help ordinary people feel better equipped to offer safe, informed support.The 100,000-certificate milestone represents the reach of a programme that seeks to make mental-health support a shared responsibility rather than something left exclusively to professionals. In April 2026, Born This Way Foundation launched its Generation Be There campaign to expand participation and encourage more people to complete the course. The campaign works with organisations and community partners to bring the programme to young people and the adults who support them.The foundation’s impact timeline said the initiative had more than 186 partners and over 590 attendees across campaign events as it reached the 100,000-certificate milestone. Its activities included events, discussions and outreach designed to encourage people to move beyond simply discussing mental health and learn practical ways to help. The course has also received recognition from the digital and communications industries. The foundation lists the Be There Certificate among the recipients of a 2023 Gold Anthem Award, a 2023 Shorty Award and a 2023 Webby Honoree distinction.The initiative reflects a broader approach to youth wellbeing: building communities in which people feel comfortable discussing mental-health struggles and seeking help. Friends, classmates, colleagues and family members may notice changes in someone's behaviour before that person approaches a professional, making informed and compassionate responses important. However, recognising distress does not mean diagnosing a condition. The course encourages participants to listen, express concern and understand when further assistance is needed.For Gaga and Germanotta, the foundation has provided a platform to extend their message of acceptance into practical programmes. The latest milestone proves that the message has reached a substantial international audience, with the certificate offering participants a structured way to learn how to respond when someone needs support.
Article Summary: The Born This Way Foundation was co-founded by Lady Gaga and her mother, Cynthia Germanotta, in 2012. In May 2026, the foundation announced that more than 100,000 Be There Certificates had been earned worldwide. The certificate programme teaches participants how to recognise signs of distress, respond with care and help someone connect with appropriate support. The initiative focuses on turning conversations about mental health into practical action.

Article Title: In 1917, a Utah businessman found that transporting bricks by road was too expensive; he sent them through the postal system instead, until the sheer volume forced the US government to intervene
Article Text:
Coltharp exploited postal rates, shipping individually wrapped bricks in 50-pound boxes to build his Utah bank.

When the postal service was a shipping network

A cheaper way to build a bank

The post office starts to strain

A new rule closes the loophole

In the early days of America's Parcel Post system it seemed everything that could fit within the rules was fair game for delivery. Farmers sent crops, families sent food and household goods, and businesses soon discovered that the postal network could be an unexpectedly cheap alternative to traditional freight. But in Utah, one businessman took the idea much further and used the mail to ship thousands of bricks for an entire bank.According to the Smithsonian National Postal Museum, on January 1, 1913, Parcel Post officially began, changing the way Americans could ship items. The service was particularly popular with rural families who had to haul goods into towns with express offices before they could be sent on. The new system linked packages straight to rural mailboxes, and it was nearly instantly popular. In the first half of the year, some 300 million parcels were processed. The weight limits increased quickly, from 11 pounds to 20 pounds, then eventually 50 pounds.The service was not limited to normal household parcels. Eggs, butter, vegetables and other common commodities were regularly sent through the mail, and the need for specially designed packaging arose.A report by the Medium states that in 1916, William Horace Coltharp, who had helped build the Bank of Vernal in Utah, had a strange transportation problem.The decorative pressed bricks he wanted were made by the Salt Lake Pressed Brick Company, which was about 125 miles away in a straight line. However, in the mountainous landscape, conventional transport was much more complicated. Medium reports that shipping the bricks by normal freight routes would cost more than four times their value. Coltharp looked to Parcel Post as a cheaper alternative.Postal rates were determined by the actual distance between places not the much longer route freight had to travel. Coltharp used the difference to have individual bricks wrapped and packed in boxes of about 50 pounds each, for mailing.What started as a brilliant way to save money quickly became a logistical nightmare. Thousands of bricks started arriving at Vernal, and the local postal operation was overwhelmed.In the end, Coltharp sent about 15,000 bricks, for a total shipment of some 37.5 tons, or 75,000 pounds, according to Medium. At the height of construction, the Vernal post office was already handling some two tons of mail daily, so the brick deliveries were particularly taxing.The Smithsonian National Postal Museum estimates the shipment weighed 40 tons, and Salt Lake City and Vernal postmasters and the Uintah Railroad, which hauled the parcels, were overwhelmed by the deliveries.Ultimately, the extraordinary shipment forced federal officials to rethink how Parcel Post could be used. The Post Office Department ruled that no one sender could send more than 200 pounds of parcels to one recipient in a single day.But by then Coltharp’s unconventional approach to building had already served its purpose. The bricks were sent from Salt Lake City to Vernal, piece by piece, by postal service.The episode became one of the most memorable illustrations of how a new public service could be stretched far beyond its intended purpose, and how quickly an inventive shortcut could expose the limits of the system itself.Images Courtesy: Smithsonian National Postal Museum and isock
Article Summary: In 1916, William Horace Coltharp used the postal service to ship 75,000 pounds of bricks to build a bank in Utah. The postal service was overwhelmed by the huge shipment. The episode became one of the most memorable illustrations of how a new public service could be stretched far beyond its intended purpose.

Article Title: A Virginia wildlife centre wants to help injured bald eagles fly again, but a neighbouring restaurant owner’s opposition to its proposed aviary has triggered an eight-year legal battle that has cost b
Article Text:
Why the Virginia wildlife centre wants a larger aviary

How a shared road fuelled the dispute

What the courts have decided

The financial cost of the legal battle

An injured eagle highlights the need for flight space

A wildlife rehabilitation centre in Virginia wants to build a larger aviary where injured bald eagles can regain their strength and practise flying before returning to the wild. But the proposed facility has become the centre of a bitter dispute with a neighbouring restaurant owner, turning disagreements over traffic, noise and access to a shared private road into a prolonged legal battle. The conflict involving the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center of Roanoke and restaurant owner Stan Seymour has stretched across several years, with legal fees for both sides reportedly reaching around $700,000, according to The Washington Post. While the centre says the enclosure is necessary for rehabilitating large birds of prey, Seymour has challenged the expansion over its potential impact on the surrounding neighbourhood.The Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center of Roanoke is a nonprofit rehabilitation facility that treats thousands of injured and sick wild animals each year. It cares for native wildlife, including bald eagles and other birds of prey, with the aim of returning them to their natural habitats.The centre was established by Sabrina and Lucky Garvin, who began rehabilitating animals at home before expanding their operation. Chester Leonard, the centre's executive director, has helped lead its work as it has grown into a wildlife hospital serving western Virginia.The proposed raptor building would provide a larger flight enclosure for recovering birds. After an injury, a bird of prey may need more than medical treatment to survive in the wild again. It must rebuild its strength, stamina and flying ability before it can be safely released.The centre says its existing 50-foot flight pen is not long enough to provide the conditioning large eagles need, and that a flight enclosure of at least 100 feet would be more suitable.The legal conflict escalated in 2018, when the centre sought permission to build the aviary. Access to its property runs along Coleman Road, a narrow, partly unpaved private road that crosses neighbouring properties. The road is governed by an easement dating back to the 1930s, making access rights a central issue in the dispute.Seymour, who owns 14 Bojangles fried-chicken restaurants in Virginia, has argued that the centre's expansion would bring additional traffic and noise to the area where he and his wife, Jane, live. He has also questioned whether the centre should have been permitted to operate at that location.Roanoke County approved a special-use permit for the proposed raptor building in 2018. Seymour and other neighbours challenged the decision, arguing that the centre's operations affected their properties and access to the shared road.The disagreement subsequently widened into a series of legal disputes involving zoning decisions, road access and allegations of misconduct. The parties have offered sharply different accounts of the conflict, with the centre maintaining that the litigation has hindered its rehabilitation work and Seymour arguing that his objections concern the impact of the expansion on the neighbourhood.In June 2022, the Virginia Supreme Court ruled on a challenge brought by Seymour and other neighbours against the Roanoke County Board of Supervisors. The court reversed a lower court's dismissal of their case on standing grounds, allowing them to pursue their challenge.The decision did not establish that the wildlife centre was operating unlawfully or confirm that every allegation made by the neighbours was true. It addressed whether they had sufficiently alleged harm to challenge the county's decision.The wider conflict has included allegations of road obstruction, harassment, defamation and interference with the centre's operations. The centre has accused neighbours of actions intended to disrupt its work, while Seymour has denied allegations made against him. These claims form part of the competing accounts surrounding the dispute and should not be treated as proven findings.In a report published on May 23, 2026, The Washington Post said two major cases remained unresolved at that time, leaving the future of the proposed expansion uncertain.The dispute has also become expensive for both sides. According to The Washington Post, Seymour had spent approximately $450,000 on legal fees, while the wildlife centre had spent around $230,000. Together, the costs amounted to roughly $680,000, or about $700,000.The financial burden is particularly significant for the centre, which operates as a nonprofit dependent on donations and community support. In June 2022, it said its legal expenses had already exceeded $140,000 and warned that further litigation would add to the pressure on its finances.The consequences for rehabilitation became apparent in September 2025, when the centre received a bald eagle that had been injured in a territorial fight with younger eagles. The bird was exhausted and also showed signs of lead poisoning.According to the centre, the eagle made progress in its 50-foot flight pen but needed a longer enclosure to regain the strength and endurance required for release. Unable to provide the final stage of flight conditioning at its own facility, the centre transferred the bird to the Wildlife Center of Virginia for further treatment and rehabilitation.The eagle underwent treatment for lead poisoning and additional flight exercises. After being cleared for release, it was returned to the wild at Smith Mountain Lake Community Park on October 14, 2025.
Article Summary: The Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center of Roanoke is a nonprofit rehabilitation facility that treats thousands of injured and sick wild animals each year. It cares for native wildlife, including bald eagles and other birds of prey, with the aim of returning them to their natural habitats. The proposed raptor building would provide a larger flight enclosure for recovering birds. The centre says its existing 50-foot flight pen is not long enough to provide the conditioning large eagles need, and that a flight enclosure of at least 100 feet would be more suitable.

Article Title: Meet Hollie Tang, the California high school student who built a camera-based system to control computers with tongue movements and eye blinks, then won the top $10,000 IEEE Presidents' Scholarship in
Article Text:
Hollie Tang's technology enables users to navigate devices through tongue movements and eye blinks (Photo: IEEE)

How Tang's tongue-controlled system work?

What inspired Tang to create Tonguage

Two other students recognised for their inventions

A California high school student has won the top $10,000 IEEE Presidents’ Scholarship for 2026 after developing a system that allows people with movement-related disabilities to control computers and other devices using their tongue and eye movements.Hollie Tang, a sophomore at Wilson High School in Hacienda Heights, created Tonguage, a camera-based technology that can be used to operate a computer, control a wheelchair and perform other tasks without using hands. Her project received the award at the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF), held in Phoenix in May.Tang was among three students recognised for developing technologies that could help people with disabilities or improve access to difficult environments. The awards were presented by 2026 IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall during the science fair.According to Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, Tang wanted to develop a technology that people could use without buying expensive equipment. Her system works with a standard laptop camera and does not require sensors to be implanted in or attached to the body.The project addresses a problem faced by many people with limited physical movement.According to the World Health Organisation, more than one billion people worldwide, or around 16% of the global population, live with some form of disability. For some, using a conventional keyboard, mouse or other control device can be difficult.Tang's invention uses computer vision, a technology that allows computers to interpret information captured by cameras. Her system tracks tongue movements and eye blinks, converting them into instructions that digital devices can understand.One feature is a tongue-based directional control that works like a computer cursor. Users can move their tongue to control direction, while blinking their eyes allows them to make selections, much like clicking a mouse.The technology can identify the tongue's position, direction and movement patterns. It also uses other facial signals to understand what the user wants to do. The project describes this approach as a multimodal human-machine interface, meaning it combines different forms of input to control a device.Tang also included a safety feature that identifies the intended user. If another person enters the camera's view, the system is designed to ignore that person's movements. This is particularly important when the technology is used to control a powered wheelchair, where an incorrect command could affect movement.According to a project overview published on Fairfolio, Tonguage has been developed for several applications, including typing, cursor control, powered wheelchairs and robotic arms. The system uses a common recognition and control framework across these applications.Tang initially planned to create an alternative to a keyboard and mouse. However, while researching the difficulties faced by people with motor disabilities, she realised that the technology could be useful for several other activities.Apart from helping users operate wheelchairs and robotic arms, she wanted the system to support gaming and entertainment.“We’re so focused on trying to give people autonomy over just basic human tasks that we often leave out things like gaming,” she told IEEE Spectrum. “They deserve the freedom to play games and enjoy entertainment as well,” she added.Keeping the technology affordable was another important part of her work. Instead of depending on specialised equipment, she designed it to work with cameras commonly available on laptops.“Mobility conditions don’t discriminate. They can affect anyone of any income, gender, and socioeconomic status,” she said.Tang, who hopes to study biomedical engineering, said visiting a rehabilitation centre helped her better understand the people who could benefit from her invention.“Including empathy in your technological solution is so important. Empathy is hard to teach in a classroom, but it can be learned through experience, and through actually meeting people whose lives your work might change,” she said.Tang received the top scholarship, but two other high school students were also recognised at the fair. Partap Sidhu, a junior at Bethpage High School in New York, secured second place and a $600 scholarship for NeuroGait, a lower-limb exoskeleton controlled by brain signals.His system uses an electroencephalogram (EEG) headset to detect electrical activity associated with intended movement. A convolutional neural network (CNN) interprets these signals and sends instructions to a 3D-printed exoskeleton fitted with pneumatic artificial muscles.According to Sidhu's results from 500 trials, the system achieved 95.2% accuracy in converting brain signals into physical movements. He developed the device for approximately $276.Third place went to Calvin Shang Hung, a sophomore at El Cerrito High School in California, who received $400 for developing a six-legged robot designed to travel across difficult terrain.Inspired by planetary rovers and later by disaster situations, Hung designed the robot to move through unstable areas, including collapsed buildings. Its walking system keeps three legs on the ground while the other three move, helping maintain stability.Tang's $10,000 scholarship will be paid over four years of undergraduate study. All three students also received complimentary IEEE student memberships. The scholarship programme, established by the IEEE Foundation and administered by IEEE Educational Activities, recognises high school students for their work in engineering, computer science and related fields.
Article Summary: Hollie Tang created Tonguage, a camera-based technology that can be used to operate a computer, control a wheelchair and perform other tasks without using hands. Her project received the award at the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF), held in Phoenix in May. Two other students were also recognised for their inventions.

Article Title: A Tennessee woman inherited her brother's house, then found strangers living there after a fake heir sold it while she was abroad; a court has revived her fraud claim against the title company, but no
Article Text:
A woman posing as "Dorothy Chestnut" falsely claimed to be the sole heir to the property. (AI image)

Fake documents used to sell the house

Chesnut sued company handling the sale

What Appeals court said

A Tennessee appeals court has revived the fraud claim of a woman who discovered, after returning to the United States from abroad in 2021, that the house she had inherited from her late brother had been sold without her knowledge using a fake identity and forged documents. A woman using a fake identity had claimed to be the rightful heir. In its Thursday ruling, the court allowed Barbara Chesnut to pursue her fraud claim against the company involved in the sale but upheld the dismissal of her negligence claim.According to court records , Chesnut had acquired the house in Cottontown, Tennessee, in 2012 after her brother, James Upchurch, died without leaving a will. His estate was divided among several heirs, and Chesnut arranged to buy the property using her inheritance along with additional funds. She lived in the house before moving to the United Arab Emirates around the time the estate proceedings were being completed.While she moved overseas, Chesnut continued to use the Tennessee property as her permanent address and stayed there whenever she visited the United States. Between 2013 and 2014, she also allowed two people to live in the house. One of them was Vickie Podczervinski. Both occupants left sometime between 2016 and 2017, after which Chesnut returned and stayed for several months.She eventually went back to the UAE. When the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted international travel, she was unable to return to the United States for a considerable period.
